The Yellow-edged lyretail (Variola louti) is a large-bodied serranid that inhabits coral reef slopes and outer lagoon channels across the Indo-Pacific region. Based on length-frequency distributions collected from fishery-independent surveys across the Great Barrier Reef, this grouper attains a maximum recorded total length of 83 centimeters [Li = 83 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of the genus Variola. Comparatively, most congeneric species exhibit asymptotic lengths roughly 15 to 25 percent shorter, suggesting that V. louti occupies a distinct ecological niche targeting relatively large prey items such as schooling teleosts and benthic crustaceans. Regional variation in ultimate size appears modest, with individuals from the central Pacific generally reaching comparable dimensions to those sampled from the Coral Sea. Growth trajectories fitted to otolith-derived age data indicate that the species follows a relatively slow growth pattern typical of many epinephelids, with the largest specimens representing decades of accumulated somatic investment. This large body size is accompanied by a substantial ultimate wet weight of 7155 grams [Wwi = 7155 grams], estimated from length-weight relationships developed specifically for this species across its geographic range.

Sexual maturation in Variola louti occurs at a body size considerably smaller than the ultimate maximum, reflecting the typical protogynous life-history pattern observed in many serranids. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected throughout the year reveals that females first exhibit cortical alveolar oocytes upon reaching a total length of approximately 47.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 47.6 centimeters], which corresponds to the length at puberty for this species. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 1327 grams [Wwp = 1327 grams]. The attainment of reproductive maturity at roughly 57 percent of the maximum length suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises an extended reproductive lifespan following a moderate juvenile period, a pattern that aligns with the relatively low natural mortality rates documented for large-bodied reef fishes. Individuals transitioning through puberty display a distinct acceleration in gonadosomatic index, which rises sharply from values near 0.5 percent in immature fish to approximately 3.5 percent in actively vitellogenic females. This maturation schedule implies that females typically reproduce for many years before any potential sex change.

Reproductive output in the Yellow-edged lyretail has been characterised using histological counts of hydrated oocytes from gravid females captured on the spawning grounds. Field collections conducted at a stable water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] indicate that spawning females produce a mean of approximately 3836 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3836 eggs per spawning event], based on volumetric estimates from subsamples of ovarian tissue. Individuals engage in roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day] during the peak of the reproductive season, which extends from October through February in the Southern Hemisphere. This reproductive schedule yields a maximum reproductive rate that reflects the high fecundity typical of groupers that broadcast spawn into the water column. The reproductive output per spawning event is substantially greater than that reported for smaller serranids such as Cephalopholis species, consistent with the allometric scaling of fecundity with body size. Spawning aggregations form predictably at specific reef promontories during the new moon phase, with individuals migrating up to several kilometres to reach these sites.

The early life stages of Variola louti are characterised by a pelagic larval phase that follows a brief period of yolk dependency. Eggs fertilised through broadcast spawning events develop rapidly at the prevailing water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], with hatching occurring at approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] after fertilisation. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly 0.76 millimeters. These tiny prolarvae are entirely lecithotrophic for the first several days post-hatching, relying on endogenous yolk reserves while the mouth and digestive tract complete morphological differentiation. The onset of first exogenous feeding typically occurs around day 4 after hatching, coinciding with yolk-sac resorption and the development of functional jaws. Pelagic larvae drift in the plankton for an extended period, during which they feed on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton. This lengthy dispersal phase facilitates connectivity among geographically separated reef populations.

Maximum longevity in Variola louti has been estimated through analysis of sectioned otoliths collected from commercially landed fish across multiple locations in the Indo-Pacific. At a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], individuals have a documented lifespan of 40 years [am = 40 years], which is among the highest recorded for serranids of this body size. This extended lifespan, equivalent to approximately 14600 days, allows multiple decades of reproductive activity following the attainment of maturity. The species exhibits clear growth zone increments in sagittal otoliths, with annual periodicity validated through marginal increment analysis and oxytetracycline marking experiments. Older individuals, particularly those exceeding 30 years, display markedly slowed somatic growth rates, approaching the asymptotic length asymptotically. This extended longevity has significant implications for fisheries management, as the species is particularly vulnerable to overexploitation due to its slow growth, late maturation, and the formation of predictable spawning aggregations that are easily targeted by fishers.
